metadata.title: Digital inequality in Austria: Empirical evidence from the survey of the OECD “Programme for the International Assessment of Adult Competencies”

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the Austrian PIAAC 2011/2012 microdata and restricts the analytic sample to employed and self-employed respondents who both passed the ICT core stage and completed the PSTRE (digital problem solving) assessment. The authors state that all data work and estimation were conducted in R using the svyPV package, which is designed to account for plausible values and survey weights in complex test survey designs; however, the manuscript does not report the specific weight variable name(s) from the PIAAC SUF. For the PSTRE regression, plausible values are handled via svyPV (PV-aware estimation), but the paper does not provide enough detail to confirm whether the authors applied student/sampling weights explicitly beyond what svyPV does internally. For the Eurostat time-series component (2012–2019), the paper uses aggregated descriptive shares and does not describe any PV/weight variable usage, so weighting strategy is not documented for that part.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not report a missing-data strategy for the PIAAC PSTRE regression (e.g., whether missing covariates were imputed or cases were excluded beyond the stated PSTRE/ICT-stage restrictions). This is a reporting gap because PIAAC background variables and derived indices can have item nonresponse, and the authors use a PV-aware survey estimation workflow (svyPV), which typically requires explicit documentation of how missingness is handled. The Eurostat component is descriptive and excludes some respondents based on internet-use assessment, but it still does not specify a formal missing-data handling protocol for all variables used in the time-series comparisons.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: From the Austrian PIAAC 2011/2012 survey (ages 16–65), the authors keep only respondents with proven ICT knowledge who took part in the PSTRE (digital problem solving in technology-rich environments) assessment. They exclude people with insufficient ICT skills (never used a computer, failed the ICT core stage) and those who refused the PSTRE assessment. They further restrict the sample to employed and self-employed respondents, yielding 2542 observations (1303 men, 1239 women). For the Eurostat trends, they restrict to individuals with assessable digital skills and exclude those whose digital skills could not be assessed because they reported not having used the internet in the last 3 months prior to interview.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2011/2012 Austria (16–65) PSTRE digital problem solving
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (OLS regression coefficients and statistical significance reported; no ML metrics such as RMSE/R² for predictive models).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2011/2012 Austria the study leveraged Gender, Books at home (age 16), Age, Years of schooling, and ICT use at home index to model PSTRE digital problem solving scores, finding that women score lower than men on average and that higher socio-economic background (books at home) is associated with higher PSTRE scores, with age negatively related and schooling positively related. This indicates that strengthening ICT familiarity and digital-skill support for socio-economically disadvantaged groups and women may reduce digital inequality in the Austrian workforce, though the direction of causality cannot be inferred from the cross-sectional regression.

data.outcome_summary: The paper analyzes digital inequality in Austria using the OECD PIAAC 2011/2012 survey, focusing on the PSTRE (digital problem solving in technology-rich environments) cognitive domain. The analytic sample includes employed and self-employed respondents aged 16–65 who have proven ICT knowledge and completed PSTRE (N=2542; Austria only). The authors estimate a linear regression (OLS) with PV-aware survey estimation via the R svyPV package, reporting coefficient estimates and significance rather than ML performance metrics. Key results show women’s PSTRE scores are lower by about 7.36 points on average, and PSTRE increases with socio-economic background measured by books at home at age 16; age is negatively associated and years of schooling positively associated. When ICT use in everyday life is added, gender becomes statistically insignificant and only the highest socio-economic category remains significant, suggesting ICT familiarity is closely linked to PSTRE but causality is unclear. The study also uses Eurostat ICT-use and self-reported digital-skill trends (2012–2019) descriptively, which is not directly comparable to PSTRE and may reflect response bias.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an empirical regression-based study (OLS with PV-aware survey estimation) and a descriptive time-trend analysis; it does not train or evaluate machine-learning predictive models. Consequently, ml_techniques are intentionally left empty and no ML primary model or ML metrics are available. The extraction therefore focuses on the econometric relationships reported for PSTRE and the descriptive Eurostat trends, rather than on an ML prediction pipeline.
